statement: Each imaging modality runs on a distinct physical principle that dictates both what it sees and its harm profile: ionising EM photons (X-ray/CT, DNA-damaging), non-ionising mechanical sound waves (ultrasound, no radiation), nuclear magnetic resonance of protons (MRI, no radiation), and radioactive tracer decay (nuclear/PET, internal dose, images function not anatomy).
effect_size: Foundational: the image and the hazard are the same physical agent (e.g. for CT, the diagnostic photon is the ionising one).

provenance.primary: Radiological physics fundamentals (electromagnetic spectrum; nuclear spin/Zeeman; positron annihilation)

canon_link: bucket-canon/02-physics/ (EM spectrum, nuclear spin, radioactive decay)
confidence_notes: Settled physics. Ties imaging to the physics fundamentals in 01-foundations.md.

statement: Ionising radiation at high doses is an established, uncontested human carcinogen (atomic-bomb survivor Life Span Study and other high-dose cohorts).
effect_size: Clear dose-dependent excess cancer at high doses; the anchor from which low-dose models are extrapolated.

provenance.primary: BEIR VII (National Research Council); LSS atomic-bomb survivor cohort

confidence_notes: Uncontested at high dose. The dispute is only at the low (CT-scale) end (see LNT claim).

statement: At CT-scale low doses, the linear no-threshold (LNT) model used in radiation protection is a regulatory assumption extrapolated downward from high-dose data, not a directly measured fact; whether low-dose risk is truly linear, has a threshold, or is even mildly hormetic is genuinely contested among radiobiologists.
effect_size: Per-scan individual excess lifetime cancer risk is small (order 1-in-1,000 to 1-in-10,000), and cannot be resolved at the individual level by available data.

provenance.primary: LNT model debate; BEIR VII vs hormesis literature

confidence_notes: Conflict-open. LNT is the prudent operating assumption for population protection (ALARA), but is not proven at the bottom of the dose range. Cross-ref 09-exposures-environment.md.

statement: Cumulative ionising-radiation dose from CT scans in childhood/adolescence is associated with a dose-dependent increase in subsequent cancer: leukaemia and brain tumours (Pearce UK cohort), ~24% higher overall cancer incidence (Mathews, 680,000 young Australians), and an excess relative risk ~1.96 per 100 mGy for haematological malignancies (EPI-CT, 948,174 Europeans, ~1-2 extra blood cancers per 10,000 children scanned).
effect_size: EPI-CT ERR 1.96 (95% CI 1.10-3.12) per 100 mGy for haematological malignancies; Mathews overall cancer IRR ~1.24.
population: Children/young adults scanned <22y; UK, Australia, 9 European countries

provenance.primary: Pearce et al., Lancet 2012; Mathews et al., BMJ 2013; Bosch de Basea et al. (EPI-CT), Nat Med 2023

confidence_notes: cohort-tier. Indication-bias confound (sicker children get scanned; underlying illness may raise cancer risk) is addressed by authors but not fully eliminable. Pearce DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(12)60815-0; Mathews DOI 10.1136/bmj.f2360. Justifies ALARA and pediatric preference for ultrasound/MRI.

statement: Modelling the ~93 million CT examinations performed in the US in 2023 projects ~103,000 future radiation-induced cancers over exposed patients' lifetimes; if current utilisation and dose persist, CT-associated cancer could eventually account for ~5% of all new annual US cancer diagnoses.
effect_size: ~103,000 projected lifetime cancers (90% UL 96,400-109,500); sensitivity range 80,000-127,000. Abdomen/pelvis CT in adults = 37% of projected cancers.
population: US population, 2023 CT utilisation (61.5M patients, 93M exams)

provenance.primary: Smith-Bindman R et al., JAMA Intern Med 2025

confidence_notes: A risk MODEL (BEIR-VII coefficients x measured dose distributions), not a counted body burden. The central honest point: CT harm is a problem of population volume, not single-scan injury. Depends on LNT being approximately valid at low dose.

statement: Broad imaging predictably produces incidental findings (incidentalomas) whose prevalence varies enormously by modality: <5% for chest CT (incidental PE) and whole-body PET, but >1/3 of cardiac MRIs, chest CTs and CT colonography, and ~22% of brain/spine MRIs; malignancy within an incidentaloma ranges from <5% (brain/adrenal/parotid) to ~25% (renal/thyroid/ovarian) to ~42% (breast). Most incidentalomas in healthy people are benign noise that still trigger costly cascades.
effect_size: Umbrella review of 20 systematic reviews / 240 primary studies; prevalence and malignancy rates quantified by modality and organ.

provenance.primary: O'Sullivan JW, Muntinga T, Grigg S, Ioannidis JPA, BMJ 2018 (umbrella review)

confidence_notes: meta-tier. The quantitative backbone of the 'more imaging = more problems' point. High between-study heterogeneity (I2>50% in 15/20 meta-analyses) noted. Harm is the downstream cascade, not the lesion.

statement: Whole-body MRI of healthy asymptomatic volunteers finds an abnormality in ~29% and a clinically significant finding in ~13%, with prevalence rising with age and BMI - an engine for manufacturing patients when marketed as a consumer screen.
effect_size: 148 healthy volunteers: 29.1% abnormal scans, 12.8% clinically significant; obese OR 5.4 (CI 2.1-14.0) for an incidental abnormality.

provenance.primary: Healthy-volunteer whole-body MRI incidental-findings study, Eur J Radiol 2009

confidence_notes: cohort-tier. Demonstrates the base-rate problem behind consumer whole-body MRI (Prenuvo). Cross-ref 07 §6.

statement: Whole-body MRI marketed as routine screening for the average-risk worried-well (e.g. Prenuvo) has no RCT evidence of a mortality benefit and reliably produces incidentalomas, downstream procedures, cost and anxiety; in expectation the diffuse harm exceeds the vivid rare benefit. It is reasonable only in specific high-risk genetic syndromes (e.g. Li-Fraumeni TP53 carriers).
effect_size: No mortality RCT; predictable high incidentaloma yield with low positive predictive value in low-prevalence populations.

provenance.primary: Incidental-findings literature (O'Sullivan BMJ 2018; healthy-volunteer WB-MRI 2009); USPSTF screening framework

confidence_notes: Matches the §07 verdict on executive/whole-body scans. Guideline-indicated WB-MRI surveillance in Li-Fraumeni is the narrow legitimate exception. 'A scan is not a checkup.'

statement: Image-guided endovascular mechanical thrombectomy for acute large-vessel ischaemic stroke roughly halves disability versus medical therapy alone (number-needed-to-treat ~2.6 to reduce disability by one level) - interventional radiology as definitive, RCT-proven therapy, where imaging is the lever not the predictor.
effect_size: HERMES pooled analysis of 5 RCTs; NNT ~2.6 to reduce disability one mRS level; one of the largest effect sizes in acute medicine.
population: Acute ischaemic stroke with large-vessel occlusion

provenance.primary: Goyal M et al. (HERMES collaboration), Lancet 2016

confidence_notes: meta/rct-tier, hard disability endpoint. The flagship example that image-guided intervention delivers a genuine outcome. Cross-ref 22-disease-cardiometabolic-renal.md (stroke).

statement: Interventional radiology uses imaging (fluoroscopy/ultrasound/CT) to guide needles, catheters and wires to perform through a pinhole what once required open surgery (angioplasty/stenting, aneurysm coiling, embolisation, ablation, drainage, biopsy, TIPS, uterine-artery embolisation), with markedly less trauma, shorter recovery and lower complication rates than the operations it replaces.
effect_size: Procedure-specific; field-defining since Dotter's 1964 angioplasty. Often local anaesthesia, same-day, organ-sparing.
population: Patients with vascular, oncologic, hepatobiliary, and haemorrhagic conditions

provenance.primary: Charles Dotter (transluminal angioplasty, 1964); modern IR practice (SIR)

confidence_notes: Evidence is procedure-specific (thrombectomy is RCT-tier; others range cohort to RCT). An under-appreciated, high-leverage field where imaging is therapeutic.

statement: AI (deep learning) reaches radiologist-level accuracy on narrow, well-defined imaging detection tasks (diabetic retinopathy, large-vessel occlusion, chest X-ray triage, tumour segmentation); AI-supported mammography (MASAI RCT) increased cancer detection ~29% with no significant rise in false positives and ~44% less reading workload.
effect_size: MASAI: detection 6.4 vs 5.0 per 1000 (ratio 1.29, 95% CI 1.09-1.51); workload -44%; FP not significantly increased.
population: >100,000 women in population breast screening (MASAI); narrow-task benchmark datasets

provenance.primary: Lang K et al. (MASAI), Lancet Oncol 2023 (full analysis 2025); IDx-DR/LumineticsCore FDA authorisation 2018

confidence_notes: rct-tier for the augmentation use. Honest caveat: extra MASAI yield included small in-situ (DCIS) disease (overdiagnosis question) and the PRIMARY interval-cancer/mortality endpoint is still in follow-up. More detection not yet proven to be more benefit.

statement: AI imaging performance on benchmark datasets does not equal deployment benefit: thousands of 'AI matches radiologists' papers exist but only a handful of prospective outcome trials; models routinely degrade on external data (distribution shift), and automation bias/deskilling are live risks. AI is shaping up as a tool that augments radiologists, not one that replaces them (contra Hinton's 2016 'stop training radiologists' prediction).
effect_size: External-validation gap well-documented; radiologist demand rose, not fell, in the decade after the 2016 replacement prediction.

provenance.primary: External-validation literature; Geoffrey Hinton 2016 prediction; cross-ref 33-public-health-systems.md §6

confidence_notes: Conflict-open on replacement-vs-augmentation. The detection task is the easy part; the decision the image feeds is the hard part.

statement: A large fraction of imaging is low-value: early MRI for acute low-back pain without red flags finds disc bulges present in most pain-free adults, leads to more surgery, and does not improve outcomes; CT for uncomplicated headache, routine pre-op chest X-rays, and annual whole-body CT/MRI for the asymptomatic are Choosing Wisely 'do not do' items. A scan is not a checkup.
effect_size: Choosing Wisely (ABIM Foundation + American College of Radiology + specialty societies) consensus low-value-imaging lists.

provenance.primary: Choosing Wisely campaign (ABIM Foundation, American College of Radiology)

confidence_notes: Imaging value is conditional on a specific pre-test question that changes a decision. 'More imaging = better care' is refuted. Cross-ref 07-clinical-prevention.md, 21-pain-injury-rehab.md (back pain imaging).
